# Predictive maintenance model

Code: `src/cvi/ml/` (`features.py`, `synthetic.py`, `train.py`, `model.py`), batch scoring `src/cvi/lifecycle/scoring.py`.
Artifacts: `ml/artifacts/<version>/{model.joblib,metrics.json}` + `LATEST` pointer (baked into the Docker image at build time:
`python -m cvi.ml.train`).

## Honest framing
**There is no real failure data in this project.** Training data is generated by `cvi.ml.synthetic`: a hidden per-vehicle *wear* variable
drives the observed features (hotter coolant, lower oil pressure, more DTC/overheat alerts, vibration, EV state of health, harsh driving,
service overdue) and the probability of a failure within the next 14 days; label and feature noise are added so the task is not trivial.
The metrics below therefore show that the **pipeline recovers a known synthetic structure** and beats a service-interval baseline, not
that it would predict real breakdowns. With real fleet failure labels the same code path (features → train → evaluate → version →
score) applies unchanged.

## Features (14) — identical for training and production inference
`coolant_ewma_c`, `overheat_alerts_7d`, `dtc_alerts_7d`, `low_oil_alerts_7d`, `oil_pressure_ewma_kpa`, `vibration_ewma_g`,
`battery_soh_pct` (100 for non-EV), `is_ev`, `harsh_per_100km_7d`, `idle_ratio_7d`, `km_since_service`, `days_since_service`,
`vehicle_age_years`, `health_score`.
In production they come from PostgreSQL only: slow EWMAs of raw signals maintained by the stream processor (`vehicle_health.signals`),
7-day alert counts, daily stats, the last maintenance record and model year (`FEATURE_SQL` in `scoring.py`).

## Baseline vs model
* **Baseline** (what fleets do without ML): a service-interval rule — `max(km_since_service / 30,000, days_since_service / 365)`.
* **Model**: `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` (depth 4, 300 iterations with early stopping, seed fixed).
* **Protocol**: 60,000 synthetic vehicles; stratified 60/20/20 train/validation/test split with a fixed seed; baseline and model are scored on the *same untouched
  test set*; metrics computed by `train.py`, never hard-coded.

Results of the committed run (`docs/performance/ml-metrics.json`, a copy of the artifact written by `train.py`; reproducible — a test asserts determinism; the date part of the version changes when you retrain on another day):

| metric (test set, 12,000 vehicles, 10.1% positives) | service-interval baseline | gradient-boosting model |
|---|---|---|
| ROC-AUC | 0.596 | **0.853** |
| PR-AUC (average precision) | 0.154 | **0.503** |
| precision if the workshop inspects the top 10% | 0.184 | **0.501** |
| recall at that budget | 0.182 | **0.496** |
| Brier score | — | 0.066 |

Validation-set ROC-AUC 0.854 vs test 0.853 (no sign of over-fitting to the test split).

## Explanations
`MaintenanceModel.explain` performs local sensitivity analysis: each feature is replaced by the training median and the drop in predicted
probability is the feature's *risk contribution*. The top 3 positive contributions are stored with the prediction (`top_factors`), shown in
the UI/agent ("elevated average coolant temperature (112.4)") and tested to be positive for a high-wear vehicle.

## Versioning, inference, lifecycle
* Version string `pm-<date>-<hash of data size, seed, feature list>`; every `maintenance_predictions` row stores `model_version`.
* Batch scoring (`python -m cvi.lifecycle.scoring`, or hourly in the `lifecycle` service) writes one prediction per vehicle (100,000 vehicles in the seed run);
  predictions older than 30 days are pruned; the latest per vehicle is exposed via the `latest_maintenance_predictions` view.
* Seeding creates per-vehicle `signals`/service history from the *same generator* so scoring of the seeded fleet is meaningful.
* Retraining: `make train` (+ rebuild images). Future work: drift monitoring on feature distributions, calibration check, champion/challenger.

## Related detectors (not ML)
Streaming rule/statistical detectors (EWMA z-score, windowed rules) provide the real-time alerts; the ML score ranks *future* risk.
